title: Hospitality at the bar
lead: Service is the delivery; hospitality is how it feels. Run a bar that gets both right.

read.bigIdea: Service is how it’s delivered. Hospitality is how it feels.
read.where: Danny Meyer (Union Square Hospitality Group) puts it this way: **service** describes how well the product was **delivered**; **hospitality** describes how the person receiving it **feels**. A perfect drink, on time, is service. The guest feeling looked after while it happened is hospitality. Meyer’s point: it takes **both** to be great.

stops.name: Service
stops.text: The right drink, to spec, **on time**.

read.mixup: Fast isn’t the same as warm. A drink can be perfect and the guest can still feel **ignored**.
read.sayIt: Welcome in. What are you in the mood for tonight?

keyPoints.line: every guest who sits, right away.

read.bigIdea: See the whole bar, not just the next ticket.
read.where: A bar lead watches the **whole room**. Every guest who sits gets **acknowledged** right away, even if the drink is a minute off. Watch the **pace**: an empty glass, a menu closed, a check reached for. Watch the **mood**: celebrating, talking business, wanting quiet. Serve the night the guest came for.
read.mixup: Acknowledging a guest isn’t serving them. It’s telling them they’re **seen**: “I’ll be right with you.”
read.sayIt: I see you: I’ll be right with you.

keyPoints.line: use it once you know it.
it so the whole team knows.

read.where: Regulars are the bar’s steady business. Learn their **names** and use them. Remember the **usual**, but still **ask** (“The usual, or something new tonight?”). Share what you learn with the team, so a regular is recognized on any night, not just yours.
read.mixup: Pouring the usual before they ask can feel like being taken for granted. **Offer** it.
read.sayIt: Good to see you again. The usual, or want to try the new fall drink?

keyPoints.line: it fast: remake, replace, or a manager.

read.bigIdea: Own it, fix it, follow up.
read.where: When a guest isn’t happy, **listen** to the whole thing without arguing. **Own** it (“I’m sorry, let me fix that”), then **fix** it fast: remake the drink, offer another, or bring in a manager. Check back **before they leave**. Then tell the team what happened, so it doesn’t happen twice.
read.mixup: Explaining why the drink is “supposed to taste like that” isn’t a fix. **Offer** something they’ll enjoy.
read.sayIt: I’m sorry about that. Let me make you something you’ll like better.

sources: Danny Meyer on NPR, 2006 (npr.org/transcripts/6162737); Setting the Table (HarperCollins, 2006); House practice (ours; GM to confirm). Written for Mise in our own words, Nov 12, 2026.

cards.answer: How well the product is delivered

cards.answer: Both great service and great hospitality

cards.q: A guest sits at a busy bar. You should…
cards.answer: Acknowledge them right away, even before you can serve
wrong: Wait until you’re free to say anything
Slide a menu without a word

cards.q: A guest closes the menu and looks up. That usually means…
A regular sits down. The best opener is…
cards.answer: Greet them by name and offer the usual or something new
wrong: Hand them the full menu silently
Ask for their ID card number

cards.q: Why share what you know about regulars with the team?
cards.answer: So they’re recognized on any night

cards.q: Remembering a regular’s usual means you…
cards.answer: Still ask before you make it

cards.q: A guest says their drink is too sour. You first…
After fixing a problem, you should…
cards.answer: Check back before the guest leaves
wrong: Remove the drink from the menu

cards.q: After a guest problem, the team should…
cards.answer: Hear what happened so it doesn’t happen twice
